RESPONSE_TO: CC2  
Confirmed on your round-5 note: the rebinding map for the deep-copy/Stage-4 fix should key from `new_findings` only, not `new_findings + barrier_rejected`. `barrier_rejected` are pre-triage originals and are not the population later traversed by Helper/RegT/fix-eval. Your narrowing is correct.

RESPONSE_TO: DeepSeek  
On `_compute_chain_hash()`: I agree it remains a security design limitation in the artifact, but I am not re-filing it here because it is already present in OPEN as DeepSeek_F001 and was also listed in applied-fix history as Bug #20. Under fail-closed constraints I should not duplicate an already-open finding without new evidence of a distinct regression. My stance is: should be fixed, but not re-reported by me this round.

@CC2: Your CC2_F002 on truncating `model_responses` is supported by the code. One extension: `_save_round_json()` still bypasses `_atomic_write_json()`, so a crash can leave a partially-written round file containing malformed JSON; after recovery, `load_checkpoint()` catches the parse error and silently restores empty `model_responses`, reintroducing degraded relay via a different path. That couples truncation and durability.

@Gemini: Please verify whether you also see this in `verification_chain._verify_single()`: for `storage_mode == "hash_only"`, the method never checks that `sealed_body` omits `payload`. A tampered record can carry hidden payload bytes not covered by the documented storage contract yet still verify cryptographically because `entry_hash` is recomputed over the tampered body.

@DeepSeek: Please check my F002 below against your timestamp work. `_normalize_timestamp()` claims to “preserve sub-second precision when present”, but `_utc_now()` uses second precision only. That means append/seal operations mix timestamp granularities depending on caller path, which can perturb canonicalized bodies and signatures across otherwise identical append sequences.

The verifier checks `payload_hash` only when `sealed_body["storage_mode"] == "full_payload"`, but it never enforces the inverse invariant for `hash_only`: that `sealed_body` must NOT contain a `payload` field. Evidence: `_build_sealed_body()` omits `payload` unless `storage_mode == "full_payload"`, establishing the writer-side contract. But `load_json()` accepts arbitrary record dicts, and `_verify_single()` recomputes `entry_hash` from the loaded `sealed_body` as-is. Therefore a tampered or malicious JSON chain can set `storage_mode` to `hash_only` while embedding an arbitrary `payload`; `entry_hash` and `chain_hash` will still verify if recomputed consistently, and `verify_chain()` returns valid. This breaks the documented storage semantics ('hash_only' means payload is not stored) and allows hidden payload insertion into records that are later treated as metadata-only.",

Result: two otherwise identical record/epoch creation paths serialize different timestamp granularities depending on whether the timestamp was caller-supplied or generated internally. def _utc_now() -> str:
    """Current UTC timestamp in RFC 3339 UTC, preserving sub-second precision."""
    dt = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    iso = dt.isoformat(timespec="microseconds")
    if iso.endswith("+00:00"):
        iso = iso[:-6] + "Z"
    if ".000000Z" in iso:
        iso = iso.replace(".000000Z", "Z")
    return iso
